These cues imply military/combat and sexual-threat or specific geopolitical associations that are not plausibly linked to the reported trauma, and no accompanying threat, appraisal, or strategy items provide a bridge that would make these triggers understandable for this patient. By contrast, the memory items are internally coherent and fit severe reliving after an MVC, as well as the active Memory → Triggers formulation.

'Cars hit by accident' fits the trauma and aligns with the active Memory → Triggers formulation, but 'Sexual situations or intimacy' and 'Arab villages' imply very different trauma contexts (e.g., sexual trauma or combat/terrorism-related threat) that are not represented anywhere else in Memory, Threat, Appraisals, or Strategies. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain as belonging to the same patient and trauma.

For a 51-year-old male welder whose index trauma is a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile clinically with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile. The memory items all concern vivid sensory/bodily reliving of a crash, which coheres with MVC trauma and the active Memory → Triggers edge, but 'Arab villages' implies a war-zone or ethnopolitical context that is not represented anywhere else in the self-report or formulation. This is a clearly implausible trigger for this trauma profile, unlike the crash imagery and alcohol smell triggers, which could plausibly cue MVC memories.

vignette:
The accident happened on a Tuesday evening in late November. Tane was driving home from the fabrication shop where he worked as a welder, his shoulders aching from a long shift spent bent over steel beams. He stopped at a four-way intersection, checked both ways, and started across. The other driver came from his left, running a red light at nearly fifty miles an hour. The impact hit Tane's driver-side door, spinning his truck half a turn before it came to rest against a utility pole. He remembers the smell first-the sharp, sweet stench of bourbon that poured through the shattered window from the other driver's car, mixing with the smell of gasoline and hot metal. He remembers the sound of twisting steel and breaking glass, and the way his body was pinned against the door, his ribs pressed so hard against the seat frame he thought they would crack. He remembers the helplessness of being trapped, unable to move his legs, convinced the fuel line had ruptured and the truck would explode. Emergency responders cut him out with the Jaws of Life. He spent three days in the hospital with two broken ribs, a fractured clavicle, and a deep contusion on his right thigh that still ached long after the bruises faded.

In the months that followed, Tane found that the memory of the crash did not behave like an ordinary memory. It came without warning, and when it came it was not a recollection so much as a re-inhabiting. He would be standing at his welding bench, the torch in his hand, and suddenly his body would seize as if it were back in the driver's seat-his shoulders hunching forward, his right knee pressing against an imaginary floorboard, his torso twisting toward an impact that was not there. The physical pain would return too, a sharp ache in his ribs, a deep throb in his shoulder, a heavy bruised sensation in his thigh, exactly where he had been injured, as though the crash were still happening inside his body. These episodes were not memories he observed; they were events he re-entered fully, across every sense. He could smell the bourbon, hear the screech of metal, feel the shock of the collision travel through his frame-and in the wake of this total reliving, his senses stayed locked on alert, scanning for anything in his environment that matched. The rumble of a diesel truck on the highway outside the shop would make his chest tighten. The hiss of compressed air from a colleague's pneumatic tool would send a jolt through him. A whiff of alcohol from a passerby would stop him cold, his mouth going dry, his heart hammering before his mind had registered what the smell meant. The sight of a crumpled fender in a junkyard or a dented door in a parking lot would pull him instantly back into the memory, the two images fusing until he could not distinguish what he was seeing from what he had lived through. Each trigger seemed to feed on the memory, and the memory fed back into the triggers, tightening a loop he could not find his way out of.

At work, Tane learned to manage, though the cost was mounting. He positioned his welding station with his back to the roll-up door so he would not see headlights sweep across the shop floor. He stopped taking his lunch break in the staff room because a colleague occasionally brought in a beer, and the smell, even from across the room, would set him on edge. He took a longer route home to avoid the intersection where the crash had happened, adding twenty minutes to his commute each way. His wife, Lani, noticed that he no longer wanted to drive her to the grocery store on weekends, and that he flinched when she opened a bottle of cooking wine. She did not push him on it, but her silence felt heavy, and Tane could feel a distance growing between them that he did not know how to bridge.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three weeks ago at the shop. A new apprentice had left an empty bourbon bottle in the break room trash-Tane caught the scent the moment he walked in, and before he could stop it, the memory hit him full force. He dropped to his knees behind a storage rack, his body locked in the crash position, his ribs aching, his throat tight, unable to breathe or speak for nearly a minute. His foreman found him there and insisted he see someone. Tane agreed, not because he thought talking would help, but because he was afraid that the next time it happened, he might not be able to get back up. He is afraid of what the loop is doing to him, and more afraid still that it will never stop.
